mechanism: Onlook is a desktop app that renders a canvas over a locally running app and lets a designer edit visually. Each design session runs in its own git worktree against the real codebase, an existing coding agent makes the code changes, and every result lands as a pull request that can be reviewed or discarded. The canvas is a live view of the real app, not a mockup, so the source of truth stays the code.
claim: A canvas on top of your real codebase with parallel worktrees, each change landing as a PR, rebuilt as an open-source agentic design tool.
why_not_testable: It is a desktop app that needs an installed coding agent and a project to point at, so no honest keyless 30-minute slice exists.
needs: A desktop install and a logged-in coding agent.
one_line: Onlook puts a design canvas over a live local app, one git worktree per idea, every change returning as a reviewable pull request.
idea_why: Worktree-per-variant with PR as the unit of review is a clean way to let non-engineers explore without breaking the main branch.
breakdown: Clone the repo, run it against a small local site, and open two worktrees with different design variants. Each variant is edited visually, the agent writes the code diff, and the diff is reviewed as a PR. A hired designer would do the judging between variants, since nothing here picks the better design.

mechanism: A Claude Code plugin chains yt-dlp, ffmpeg and faster-whisper. It scores candidate clip moments from loudness spikes, hype words in the transcript, YouTube's 'most replayed' heatmap and live chat message-rate spikes, then crops to 1080x1920 with captions. Campaign discovery reads pay-per-1,000-views listings on a clipping marketplace. Platforms do not pay for plain reposts, so the money depends on campaign rules, not on the clipping.
claim: Turns GTA 6 streams into paid vertical clips; campaigns pay around $1 per 1,000 views, with no income promised.
verdict_question: On one public video, do the top 5 audio-loudness peaks fall within 15 seconds of a peak in YouTube's most-replayed heatmap: how many of 5?
probe_title: Moment-finder: do loudness peaks on a public video land within 15s of YouTube's most-replayed peaks (hits out of 5)?
one_line: A GTA 6 clipping plugin picks clip moments from loudness spikes and 'most replayed' data; the question is whether those two signals agree.
idea_why: Loudness plus replay-heatmap is a plausible highlight signal, but agreement between the two has not been measured here.
breakdown: Pick one public video with a most-replayed graph, pull audio with yt-dlp, compute loudness peaks with ffmpeg, and read the heatmap markers from the page data. Compare peak times and count matches. The next step would be a transcript hype-word score from the local transcription pipeline. A human would still pick hooks and read campaign rules, since no script covers rule compliance.
tools_have: Keyless YouTube search, oEmbed and transcript pipeline
missing: Nobody has verified the payout claim; campaign rates are owner-reported.

mechanism: CAR builds a semantic knowledge graph from retrieved papers and gives an ideation agent graph-retrieval tools plus four operators: bisociation, analogy, exploration and elaboration. Each operator call must pass a structural acceptance check and is logged, which yields a trace of steps and declared sources. Output is judged against single-shot prompting and other agents on novelty and feasibility.
claim: Higher methodological novelty than single-shot prompting and The AI Scientist, but no ablation contrast survives multiple-comparison correction.
why_not_testable: Needs model answers and there is no local LLM, so it is not keyless tonight.
one_line: An ideation agent with logged 'operators' beats one-shot prompts on novelty, but its own ablation says the operators add nothing over free iteration.
idea_why: The authors' own ablation shows no corrected benefit from the explicit operators; only the traceability is a real gain.
breakdown: Retrieve abstracts on a topic through arXiv's open API, extract concept pairs into a graph, and prompt an agent to propose ideas with a log line per operator. Compare against a plain iterate-and-refine baseline and judge both blind. The judging needs a person or a second model; the trace log is the useful piece to reuse for probe writing.

missing: The authors' code is not named in the abstract.

mechanism: Reading a Reddit thread without an API key means fetching its public page or the same URL with .json appended, over plain HTTP from a script, rather than through an agent browser that refuses the domain. It depends on Reddit not rate-limiting or blocking anonymous requests with a plain user agent. The returned JSON holds post and nested comments, which can then be summarised.
claim: Agent browser routes (built-in pane, Chrome extension, WebFetch) all refuse reddit.com, so threads cannot be read by an agent.
verdict_question: Does a plain curl to a public thread's .json endpoint return HTTP 200 with comments, or a block: which status code?
probe_title: Reddit .json endpoint: does an anonymous curl to a public thread return comments (200) or a block, and how many requests before throttling?
one_line: Agent browsers refuse Reddit, but a plain script may still read a public thread as JSON; tonight's probe checks whether that door is open.
idea_why: Whether anonymous script access still works is an empirical question that one request answers.
breakdown: Send three or four polite, spaced requests for public thread .json URLs with a descriptive user agent, record status codes and comment counts, and stop at the first block. If open, wrap it in a poller that fetches threads matching keyword alerts and hands text to a summariser. If blocked, the fallback is Reddit's official API with a registered app, which needs an account a person must create.

mechanism: A skill that forces the model to name its first, most average answer and then move away from it for a project-specific reason. Scripts support it: seed.py draws random starting constraints from system randomness and a history file to avoid repeats, moves.py logs which move worked, rough.py perturbs SVG geometry to look hand-made, and check.py renders an SVG at two sizes to flag overflowing, low-contrast or tiny text.
claim: Steers Claude away from generic output in names, posters and UI, shown by comparing six plain runs against a picked bottom row.
verdict_question: Does check.py flag at least one real defect (clipped or low-contrast text) in a deliberately flawed 400x600 SVG, yes or no?
probe_title: antialgorithm check.py: does it flag clipped and low-contrast text in a deliberately flawed SVG poster (yes/no, count)?
one_line: A creative skill makes Claude name its most average answer first, then rolls random constraints to leave it; the SVG checker is the testable part.
idea_why: Forcing a named default and a random seed is a cheap, mechanical way to widen output, and the SVG lint is a plain deterministic check.
breakdown: Clone into the sandbox, run seed.py a few times and confirm seeds differ and history is respected. Hand-write a flawed SVG and run check.py to count flagged issues. Judging whether the output is actually less generic needs a person comparing batches, which no script covers.

mechanism: Database reactivation sends a timed sequence of SMS or email to a business's old leads or lapsed customers, offering a reason to come back and routing replies to a booking link or a person. It needs a client list with a lawful basis for contact (UK PECR consent or soft opt-in for existing customers), a sender number or domain, and reply handling. Revenue comes from bookings recovered, so list size and recency set the ceiling.
claim: Reactivating dormant leads books appointments; the community says it works but the results are owner-reported.
why_not_testable: Needs a client's list, a sending account and consent; nothing can be run keyless.
needs: A client with a consented list and an SMS or email sending account.
one_line: Reactivating old leads by SMS is a real mechanism, but it only works where a client has a large recent consented list.
idea_why: Contacting past customers converts better than cold prospects, provided consent is clean and the list is recent.
breakdown: Take a client's lead export, filter to contacts with consent and recent activity, then draft a three-message sequence with an opt-out in each. Send through an SMS or email platform, route replies to a booking link, and report bookings against messages sent. A person must confirm the consent basis and handle live replies.
tools_have: Claude Code with skills and sub-agents
missing: A client with a usable list and a confirmed UK consent position.

mechanism: A kernel-agnostic conformance suite of 3,487 geometry cases checks B-rep modelling operations (booleans, fillets, shells, sweeps, lofts, STEP, queries) against expected answers from closed forms and exact geometry, such as the volume of a known solid. Each kernel is wrapped in an adapter, so the same cases run on any of them. The oracle is mathematics, not another kernel's output, so it does not inherit another kernel's bugs. The kernel itself, springrep, is safe Rust written with Claude Code and tuned against that suite.
claim: A new Rust B-rep kernel passes 3,487 conformance cases that caught hundreds of bugs its own tests missed.
why_not_testable: Needs a Rust toolchain and building a kernel plus adapters, which is unlikely to fit 30 minutes keyless.
one_line: An LLM-written CAD kernel was hardened by a separate suite whose expected answers come from closed-form geometry, not from another kernel.
idea_why: Test oracles from exact maths are independent of the code under test, which is the right guard against machine-written code.
breakdown: Clone the conformance suite, read a handful of case definitions to see how expected values are derived, and recompute two by hand (a cylinder volume, a sphere with a fillet). The same pattern, closed-form oracles checked against an LLM-built implementation, could be reused for the Pitch and Grinder maths. A CAD specialist would write adapters for kernels.
